name: Eye contact practice
lead: Eye contact practice refers to deliberately training oneself to hold another person's gaze in conversation, usually to appear more confident and present. Eye contact, when two people look at each other's eyes at the same time, is a form of nonverbal communication studied as oculesics [1].

Wikipedia reports that eye contact can signal interest, forms part of flirting, and is linked in some contexts to confidence and respect, while norms differ widely between cultures [1]. Published research on structured eye contact practice as a self-improvement method is limited.

paras: Brief glances can develop into repeated eye contact that signals attraction, while unbroken staring can feel overbearing in many cultures [1]. In crowds strangers often avoid eye contact as civil inattention [1].

In East Asia and Nigeria not looking directly at a person of higher status can be respectful, whereas in Western cultures averted eyes may be read as evasive [1]. Practices vary widely within religious and social traditions [1].

People with autism spectrum disorders or social anxiety may find eye contact unsettling [1]. Social anxiety disorder is also described as involving avoidance behaviours, which can include avoiding eye contact [2]. A study of 20 five-year-olds found that children who looked away while thinking were more likely to answer correctly, suggesting faces can be mentally demanding to look at [1].
No studies found on eye contact practice as a self-improvement method. Related research on gaze in infants and learning is summarised on Wikipedia [1].

card.summary: Deliberately training steady gaze in conversation for presence; eye contact is well described, training it is unstudied.
card.note: Norms vary by culture; autistic or socially anxious people may find it distressing.

quick.overview:
Eye contact practice means training oneself to hold gaze during conversation to appear more present and confident. Eye contact itself is a well-described part of nonverbal communication.

No studies were found testing eye contact training for appearance or attractiveness goals.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners rehearse holding gaze in everyday talks. Sources note eye contact can signal interest and attraction, but meanings differ across cultures.
quick.risks: Prolonged unbroken eye contact can feel overbearing, and people with autism or social anxiety may find it unsettling. Cultural norms differ.
